scope.ages: Unchanged existing Ontario7–8 contexts; no age, new-context, topic or dependency changes.

teacherInstructions: These are original supplied-source studies and fictional decision models, not reports of local observations. Read each study card with the learner, explain unfamiliar words and discuss a worked example. Use ordinary oral explanations, drawings or writing to make reasoning accessible. Do not supply the assessed decision or reorder the learner’s model for them.

Then remove the ordered study sheet. Give the learner the separate jumbled stage tokens or decision cards listed below. The learner constructs and explains the relation; an adult may read an unordered token verbatim without giving its position. After an error, teach using the study material and later reassess with the changed case. Merely repeating a teacher’s answer is insufficient.

Assess each source requirement separately. Whole-topic checks and hard prerequisites remain separate: success here does not award all life-cycle vocabulary, all insect transformations, plant diagrams, human life stages or the complete organism–habitat repertoire. No field collection, handling wildlife, water access, hazardous-product handling or practical habitat alteration is required.

studyCases.title: One animal action can help and create a conflict
studyCases.kind: Original hypothetical model grounded in primary factual roles; not TRCA field dataset
readAloud: A beaver changes its stream habitat by building a dam; the new wetland can provide habitat for other animals.
In this model, one valued tree beside a public path has been chewed by a beaver. A responsible adult has identified a possible safety/property problem, and children stay away from the tree and water.

The responsible site team can choose selective tree protection that keeps a beaver from reaching that particular trunk while leaving other appropriate habitat and food available. The child does not fit the protection.
Model alternative R removes all trees around the pond; it would also remove habitat and food. Model alternative P protects the identified valued tree while retaining other suitable vegetation.

No flooding is occurring in this first model. A separate changed case introduces backed-up water threatening an access route; protecting a tree trunk does not control that water level. Qualified adults assess the changed flood risk and site-appropriate response; this case does not prescribe a device or dam removal.
studyCases.sourceBinding: TRCA beaver explanatory body: wetland habitat, tree/infrastructure effects, selective protection and flooding distinction. Fictional decision conditions are explicitly declared.
studyCases.limits: No source observations, learner attainment, installation instructions, legal permission, flood guarantee or universalbeaverbenefit inferred.

studyCases.title: A bee visiting flowers
readAloud: A bee visits flowers for food. During visits, pollen can stick to its body and be carried to another flower. This helps many flowering plants produce seeds and fruits. People and other animals can benefit from those plants. Some plants use wind or water or can pollinate themselves; it is not true that every plant needs bees.

Our fictional garden contains flowers that need visiting animal pollinators. The model changes only the availability of these visits, keeping water, light and suitable growing conditions the same. If visits are missing, fewer flowers in this model produce fruit. We have not measured a real garden or claimed that every crop disappears.
studyCases.sourceBinding: NPS About Pollinators, main explanatory body read 2026-11-12; facts limited to pollen transfer and plant reproduction. Fictional garden stipulation is an analytic model, not an NPS experiment.

studyCases.title: Two different human activities
readAloud: The fictional public path needs a safe accessible route. Route A would remove the particular pond-edge vegetation that the supplied animal case uses for shelter/cover. Route B follows an existing cleared area and, in this declared model, can meet access needs while retaining that vegetation.

People require access and safety; the selected pond animals require their declared shelter and food conditions. The model does not claim all real routes or restoration projects have these exact effects.
Qualified adults choose and carry out any route work; the child explains the comparison, does not enter a habitat or move animals.

A second, distinct activity in this fictional community is dumping unwanted paint or oil onto land where rainwater can carry it into the pond. These products can make the water dangerous for fish. This is pollution, not a way to dispose of waste.

The model offers an adult-managed appropriate collection route for unwanted products. Keeping them out of the pond reduces this stated pollution risk, but does not make all waste disappear or guarantee that every environmental problem is solved. Children explain the choices and tell a responsible adult; they do not touch, pour or collect the products.
studyCases.sourceBinding: Route/vegetation effects are explicitly supplied model conditions. ECCC pollution education main body 26–37,56–58,73–74 read 2026-11-12 supports the distinct pollution chain; no local disposal rule or clinical mechanism is inferred.

changedCase.facts: The existing cleared alternative is unavailable in the changed model. No other safe accessible alternative has yet been supplied.
changedCase.question: Explain why the original recommendation cannot simply be repeated as a proven solution. State the unresolved access/habitat conflict and what further qualifiedsite information is needed; do not invent a guaranteed harmless route.

facts: A female adult lays eggs on milkweed. An egg hatches into a caterpillar, the larva of the same individual.
The caterpillar crawls and eats milkweed leaves as it grows. Its striped body looks different from the winged adult.

The larva forms a chrysalis; this is the pupa stage, in which the insect transforms rather than seeking and eating leaves. A chrysalis is a pupa, not a new species; a cocoon is a covering some insects make, not a separate stage required here.
An adult butterfly emerges with wings. It flies to flowers and drinks nectar. Reproductive adults may produce the next generation of eggs.
An individual eventually dies; some individuals die before reproducing. Reproduction starts a new individuals cycle; death does not turn the same individual back into an egg.
studyCases.limits: No fixed lifespan/eggcounts/migration itinerary or legal conservation status required. No collecting/rearing animal required for this supplied-source task.

studyCases.organism: American bullfrog (museum source uses Rana catesbeiana), amphibian
facts: A female lays eggs in water. A hatchling is a tadpole of the same species; it has a tail, breathes with gills and swims.
Bullfrog tadpoles eat algae, organic material and insect larvae. They grow and develop legs.
The froglet transition has developing legs and a shrinking tail; the tail is absorbed rather than simply falling off. There is no pupa stage.
The adult has legs and no tadpole tail, breathes with lungs and moist skin, and can use its legs to swim or hop. Reproductive adults can produce the next generation of eggs.
Individuals eventually die and some do so before reproducing; offspring, not a rejuvenated dead adult, begin the next cycle.
studyCases.limits: Do not repeat AMNH egg-string wording or exact tadpole duration. Do not generalise algae-only diet or this free-swimming stage to all frogs; the museum explicitly notes exceptions. No internal reproductive mechanism or keeping wild animals required.

facts: An adult female lays eggs in a nest. The young hatch as down-covered ducklings, not tadpoles or larvae with a pupa stage.
Ducklings grow. Their later wing feathers and flight ability develop over time; newly hatched ducklings cannot yet fly.
A selected healthy, flight-capable older mallard can swim and fly. An adult female can lay eggs for the next generation. Not every individual reproduces or survives to adulthood.
The chosen duckling and adult both have a beak and two legs; their size and plumage differ. The adult does not become a different species.
Adults eventually die. Offspring start a new cycle; individual death is not hatching again.
studyCases.limits: Cornell page403blocked and not relied on. No fixed hatch/fledge ages, all-adults-always-fly assertion, hunting, legalstatus or local population claims adopted.

facts: A female gives birth to young in a nest and nurses them with milk. This selected mammal does not hatch as a caterpillar, tadpole or bird from an externally laid egg.
Newborns cannot yet see; their eyes open as they grow. Young later leave the nest and stop depending on milk. Older young and adults eat plant material.

In the selected comparison, the young cottontail is past its newborn stage, has open eyes, has fur and is leaving the nest to forage. Both this fur-covered young animal and the fur-covered adult have two ears and four legs, while the adult is larger. They remain the same species.
Some mature individuals reproduce and have a new generation of young. Individuals eventually die, and some die before reproducing.
Reproduction links the generations; death does not restart the same individual.
studyCases.limits: Dated1999 educational account, not current population/status evidence or age7–8 efficacy. Do not teach disputed naked-versus-finefur newborn wording, numerical development deadlines, animalcare instructions, disease/clinical or mating details.

materials: Unordered case labels: beaver dam, new wetland, other-animal habitat, chewed valued tree, tree safety/property conflict, bee flower visit, moved pollen, seeds/fruits, selective tree protection, remove all trees, changed flooding.
B1.1.prompt: Build two animal-action chains, using the beaver and the bee. Explain effects on the environment and on people. In the beaver tree case compare removing all trees with protecting the identified tree: choose and justify a way to reduce the negative effect while retaining suitable habitat. Then explain what changes when backed-up water threatens the path.
requiredEvidence: Distinct animal→environment→people/environment explanations from both animals.
Negative impact and cause-specific mitigation, with habitat consequence and limit.
Flooding is a different problem; protecting a trunk does not control water level, so qualified site assessment is needed.
insufficient: Teacher-selected solution repeated without a cause chain.
A claimed guarantee that one intervention solves every beaver conflict.

materials: All three environmental study cases; four blank arrows per chain; unordered cards for route clearing, loss of declared cover, animal shelter consequence, dumped paint/oil, rain transport, pond-water risk, adult appropriate collection, beaver and pollinating bee.
B1.prompt: Explain how the two animals can affect people and the environment. Separately compare how route clearing and inappropriate product disposal can affect animals and habitats. Recommend a fitting reduction for each human activity and for the tree conflict, explain a tradeoff or remaining limit, and distinguish which direction of cause each chain shows. Finally the cleared alternative route is unavailable: reassess rather than repeating your first answer.
requiredEvidence: Independent reciprocal synthesis: animal→society/environment AND two distinct human-activity→animal/habitat chains.
Benefit and negative consequence assessed using case facts, not a vote on liking wildlife.
Cause-fitting responsible action and explicit access/habitat limit; no invented harmless alternative after changed conditions.
insufficient: Only animal effects or only human effects.
A generic clean-up slogan without the stated mechanism or safe adult role.

requiredPerformance: For each species compare selected young and adult physical traits, explicitly separating at least one supplied stable feature from at least one changing physical feature. Same-species identity alone is not a physical feature.
Compare physical structure across the two species using beak/feathers versus ears/fur; do not give only names or adult group lists.
B2.1.changedCase: A child says any young bird must grow an extra pair of legs to become an adult, or that gaining flight feathers makes a duck a new species. Use the supplied stable/changing traits to correct each claim.
B2.1.delivery: Use the four readable study cards above for teaching, then remove ordered text. Supply unordered tokens separately: monarch egg/larva/pupa/adult; bullfrog egg/tadpole/legged shrinking-tail froglet/adult; mallard egg/downy nonflying duckling/older feathered bird/adult; cottontail newborn nursing young/older foraging young/adult. Read token labels without giving order. Learner makes and explains own model; reproduction arrows mean new offspring, not the same individual becoming young.

requiredPerformance: Independently describe a complete cycle for EACH required group: insect, amphibian, bird and mammal. Include the next-generation link, not only young/adult matching.
Explain a shared birth/start-growth-reproduction-death pattern and at least one meaningful difference without claiming every individual reproduces before dying.
Use a learner-created sequence/diagram or oral model; reading out the supplied ordered facts without independently reconstructing them is insufficient.
B2.3.changedCase: Identify which of two proposed diagrams is wrong when a pupa is inserted into the mallard or bullfrog cycle, explaining from the given facts rather than guessing labels.
B2.3.delivery: Use the four readable study cards above for teaching, then remove ordered text. Supply unordered tokens separately: monarch egg/larva/pupa/adult; bullfrog egg/tadpole/legged shrinking-tail froglet/adult; mallard egg/downy nonflying duckling/older feathered bird/adult; cottontail newborn nursing young/older foraging young/adult. Read token labels without giving order. Learner makes and explains own model; reproduction arrows mean new offspring, not the same individual becoming young.

requiredPerformance: Compare APPEARANCE and BEHAVIOUR through the complete cycles of the four supplied animals. For each, connect form/stage changes to changes in feeding, movement, dependence or reproduction as supplied.
Make at least one explicit cross-species comparison: radical larva/adult transformation versus more gradual bird/mammal growth; no stage-name list alone.
Explain why the same animal can change appearance/behaviour without becoming a different species.
B2.4.changedCase: A child says the chrysalis is a new animal that eats leaves like the caterpillar, and that a newly hatched duckling can fly just because adults can. Correct both stage-behaviour claims using the supplied facts.
B2.4.delivery: Use the four readable study cards above for teaching, then remove ordered text. Supply unordered tokens separately: monarch egg/larva/pupa/adult; bullfrog egg/tadpole/legged shrinking-tail froglet/adult; mallard egg/downy nonflying duckling/older feathered bird/adult; cottontail newborn nursing young/older foraging young/adult. Read token labels without giving order. Learner makes and explains own model; reproduction arrows mean new offspring, not the same individual becoming young.

B2.prompt: Make your own four-animal comparison after studying the cards. Explain how each grows and changes and how their physical characteristics distinguish them. Show one shared pattern of growth and next-generation reproduction, one stable and one changing physical feature, and compare a major transformation with more gradual growth. Connect a supplied stage-dependent movement or feeding behaviour with its body/stage. Explain why a growing animal remains the same species. Then reject the proposed claim that every animal needs a pupa stage.
requiredEvidence: All four organisms contribute evidence to an independent synthesis, not a recitation of child-code labels.
Distinct features and meaningful growth/stage changes both explained.
Cross-species similarity and difference, correct next-generation/death boundary, stage/body/behaviour connection.
B2.historicalBoundary: Actual overall core is growth/change/distinct characteristics. This does not recertify the separately retained historical B2.2 locomotion or B2.5 adaptation labels, nor add their entire repertoires to the overall by assumption.

negativeGuards: Only codes and original duty summaries/resources are published; restricted curriculum wording is omitted.

This reviewed authoring portfolio accounts for the six selected source duties. Its component associations do not certify the whole contributing topics or prerequisites; repository acceptance and downstream publication remain separate.
No historical B1.2/B2.2/B2.5 refresh inferred from a new overall. No source disposition from mere supplied facts or guided repetition.
No new topics, age lowering, missing-context creation, prerequisite deletion, learner-state compatibility claim or learner reset.
No universal all-plants-need-bees, all-mammals-livebirth, all-frogs-same-cycle, all-adult-birds-fly, all-individuals-reproduce or death-restarts-individual claims.

currentWholeCards.subject: Science
currentWholeCards.name: How Organisms Shape Habitats
currentWholeCards.description: Construct an argument supported by evidence for how plants and animals can change the environment to meet their needs
evidence: Give at least three examples of organisms changing their environment (beaver dams, bird nests, plant roots breaking rock)
Explain why organisms change their environment (to meet needs for shelter, food, water)
Construct an argument with evidence showing how a specific organism changes its environment
currentWholeCards.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how a beaver builds a dam that changes a river into a pond, or how tree roots can crack rocks apart?

currentWholeCards.subject: Science
currentWholeCards.name: Bees and pollination
currentWholeCards.description: Bees and pollination: how flowers and insects depend on each other. Bees visit flowers for nectar, pollen sticks to their bodies and transfers to the next flower. Without pollination many plants cannot make seeds or fruit. Why bees matter for the food we eat.
evidence: Describe how pollen moves from one flower to another when a bee visits to collect nectar
Explain that many fruits and vegetables depend on bees or other insects for pollination
State what would happen to a garden or farm if there were no pollinating insects
currentWholeCards.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a bee buzzing around flowers in the garden, could they explain how the bee is helping the plant — and why that matters for the food we eat?

currentWholeCards.subject: Science
currentWholeCards.name: Insect life cycles: complete metamorphosis
currentWholeCards.description: Insect life cycles — complete metamorphosis in detail. Egg → larva → pupa → adult. The larva (caterpillar, grub, maggot) looks completely different from the adult. Inside the pupa the body is rebuilt. Butterflies, beetles, flies, and ladybirds all undergo complete metamorphosis.
evidence: Name the four stages of complete metamorphosis using the correct terms: egg, larva, pupa, adult
Explain that the larva stage is when the insect eats and grows, and the pupa stage is when its body transforms
Give at least two examples of insects that undergo complete metamorphosis such as butterflies and beetles
currentWholeCards.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain the full life cycle of a beetle or butterfly using the proper words — egg, larva, pupa, adult — and tell you what happens at each stage?

currentWholeCards.subject: Science
currentWholeCards.name: Animal Body Groups
currentWholeCards.description: Describe and compare the external body structure of common animals across groups (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals)
evidence: Describe key structural features of at least three animal groups (e.g. scales, feathers, fur)
Compare two animals from different groups, noting at least two differences
Use words like 'wings', 'fins', 'legs', 'tail' correctly when describing an animal
currentWholeCards.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} describe how a fish's body is different from a bird's body and explain features like scales, feathers, or fins?

currentWholeCards.subject: Science
currentWholeCards.name: Animal Life Stages
currentWholeCards.description: Recognise that animals, including humans, have offspring which grow into adults, and describe basic animal life stages
evidence: Describe the basic life stages of a human: baby, child, teenager, adult
Give examples of other animals and their young (e.g. kitten → cat, chick → hen)
Explain that offspring grow and change as they develop into adults
currentWholeCards.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} describe how a kitten grows into a cat, or how a baby grows into an adult?

currentWholeCards.subject: Science
currentWholeCards.name: Life Cycles of Organisms
currentWholeCards.description: Develop models to describe that organisms have unique and diverse life cycles but all share the common stages of birth, growth, reproduction, and death
evidence: Describe the life cycle of at least two different organisms (e.g. butterfly, frog, plant)
Identify the common stages all life cycles share: birth, growth, reproduction, death
Explain how life cycles can look very different (metamorphosis vs gradual growth) but follow the same pattern
currentWholeCards.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} compare the life cycle of a butterfly with that of a frog and explain what stages they all share — being born, growing, having babies, and dying?
